title: The Quarter-End Illusion: The GST Sitting in Your Account Isn't Actually Yours
excerpt: The September quarter has just closed and most operating accounts look healthier than they are. A share of that balance was never trading profit, and the October BAS deadline is about to prove it.
content:
The September quarter has just closed, and for a lot of owner-led businesses the bank balance is telling a more flattering story than the real one. Three months of trading has come through, the account looks solid, and it is tempting to read that number as a straightforward measure of how the quarter went.

Part of that balance was never the business's to spend. Every invoice raised over the last three months carried a GST component collected on behalf of the tax office, and unless it has been actively separated out, it is sitting in the same account as trading profit, wages reserves and everything else. It looks like cash. For a few more weeks, until the October BAS deadline turns it into an outgoing, it behaves like cash too. Then it isn't there anymore, and whatever spending decisions were made against the fuller number have to be unwound against a thinner one.

None of this is a compliance gap. A bookkeeper or BAS agent will record and lodge that GST accurately regardless of whether it has been set aside in advance, because that is exactly the job they do well. The gap sits one layer up, in whether the business has a forward view of which dollars in the account are actually available to spend and which are already earmarked before the quarter even closes.

The Balance That Isn't All Yours

Most accounting systems will tell you the GST liability if you go looking for it, usually close to lodgement time when the BAS is being prepared. Very few owner-led businesses build a running, weekly sense of that number into how they read their bank balance day to day. The result is a single combined figure that mixes real trading cash with money that already has somewhere else to go, and every spending decision, from a stock reorder to a wage increase, tends to get made against that combined number rather than the smaller one that is actually free to use. A business carrying a healthy debtors ledger feels this even more sharply, because the GST sitting inside unpaid invoices gets counted as available before it has even been collected. Genuine cash flow discipline starts with separating those two numbers before the quarter closes, not after the BAS lands.

Why the Habit Slips Between BAS Cycles

This pattern rarely gets noticed until it repeats a few times, because each quarter it arrives the same way. Trading comes in, the balance builds, and it feels like room to move. Then the BAS deadline turns up in the same window as the superannuation guarantee payment for the same quarter, insurance renewals that tend to cluster around this time of year, and whatever stock or capacity decisions were already made against the fuller balance. None of those costs are a surprise individually. What catches businesses out is the timing collision, where several genuine obligations land in the same fortnight as a tax bill that was quietly building the whole time without a line of its own. A business that has never separated its GST from its trading cash experiences this as a sudden squeeze. A business that has been setting it aside as it goes experiences it as a payment it was already expecting.

Building a Habit That Doesn't Rely on Memory

The fix is not a more complicated reporting system. It is treating GST the way most businesses already treat superannuation and PAYG withholding, as money that belongs to someone else the moment it is collected, moved into its own place before it can be counted as spendable. A percentage of each week's receipts transferred into a separate account, reviewed as part of a rolling weekly forecast rather than discovered at BAS time, turns a quarterly shock into a number that was never really hiding. This is precisely the kind of rhythm a 13-Week Cash Flow Build is designed to create, because it forces the GST liability, the super guarantee payment and every other quarter-end obligation to sit inside the same forward view as trading income and everyday costs, rather than living in four separate mental notes.

None of this requires a bigger finance function or a more complicated chart of accounts. It requires the discipline of treating the account balance as two numbers instead of one, every week, not just when a BAS is due. For businesses that have outgrown the point where a bookkeeper's compliance view is enough and want that forward cash picture built and run properly, that is exactly the layer a fractional CFO adds on top of the compliance work already being done well. The quarter has already closed. The next one is the one still worth getting ahead of.

faqs.q: How much of my bank balance is actually GST owed to the ATO?
faqs.a: The exact figure sits in your accounting system as a GST liability, usually calculated properly when your bookkeeper or BAS agent prepares the return. The habit worth building is checking that number weekly rather than only at lodgement time, so spending decisions are made against the cash that is genuinely free to use, not the combined balance.

faqs.q: When is the September quarter BAS due for Australian SMEs?
faqs.a: Quarterly BAS for the July to September period generally falls due late in October, though the exact date depends on your lodgement method and registered agent arrangements. Your bookkeeper or BAS agent will confirm the specific deadline that applies to your business and handle the lodgement itself.

faqs.q: Should a small business keep GST in a separate bank account?
faqs.a: Many owner-led businesses find this makes the quarterly bill far less disruptive, because a portion of each week's receipts moves out of the spendable balance as it is earned rather than all at once at lodgement time. A 13-Week Cash Flow Build can set up that rhythm alongside the rest of your forecast.

faqs.q: Isn't tracking GST cash flow my bookkeeper's job already?
faqs.a: Your bookkeeper or BAS agent is doing exactly what they should be doing, which is recording and lodging your GST accurately. Building a forward view of which cash is genuinely spendable before the quarter closes is a different, strategic layer, and it is where a fractional CFO typically adds value alongside that compliance work.

faqs.q: Why does my bank balance look healthy but cash still feel tight before BAS time?
faqs.a: This is one of the most common patterns among owner-led businesses. The balance includes GST collected on sales, and often a portion of the superannuation guarantee accrual, neither of which is genuinely available to spend. Once those amounts are separated out, the real trading cash position is usually smaller, and considerably more useful to plan against.

faqs.q: Does the superannuation guarantee due date also fall around the same time as the September BAS?
faqs.a: Yes, the quarterly superannuation guarantee payment for the same July to September period generally falls due in the same late October window as the BAS, which is exactly why the two can collide if neither has been set aside in advance. Treating both as earmarked cash from the moment they accrue avoids the collision.

faqs.q: How can a fractional CFO help with quarterly tax cash flow planning?
faqs.a: A fractional CFO typically folds GST, superannuation guarantee and PAYG obligations directly into a rolling weekly cash forecast, so the business always knows which portion of its balance is genuinely free to spend. That forward visibility usually removes the quarterly surprise entirely, well before the next BAS deadline arrives.
